newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia launches new crack-down on cash economy.
newsitem.headline: Australia launches new crack-down on cash economy.

text.p: The Australian government launched a renewed effort against escalating cash economy tax evasion on Tuesday after a study estimated Canberra was losing A$4 billion to A$15 billion a year to such evasion.
"... there is a widespread acceptance in the community that not paying tax on cash is OK," a government inquiry reported on Tuesday.
"There also appears to be a perception that there is little likelihood of detection and, in any case, that the consequences of being detected are not severe."
Treasurer Peter Costello responded by promising to further exploit current anti-avoidance policies and also look at new laws to crack down on the cash economy.
"This government will put in place measures to encourage under current arrangements those transactions which are currently escaping the tax net to be picked up," Costello told parliament.
"And we will carefully examine other options to ensure that our tax system is a system that makes the cash economy and avoidance of that nature much harder to engage in in the future."
The report, prepared by tax and business officials, said the exact amount of revenue lost to such tax avoidance was unclear.
But academic studies had estimated the cash economy -- where goods or services are paid for with cash in unrecorded deals -- at 3.5 percent to 13.4 percent of gross domestic product.
That suggested A$4 billion to A$15 billion a year in lost revenue, the report said.
The study said the problem seemed to be growing.
The volume of coins and bank notes in circulation was keeping pace with the size of the economy despite the increasing use of electronic payments.
